newsitem.title: USA: NYC says spent $32 billion in FY 1996, up 1.5 pct.
newsitem.headline: NYC says spent $32 billion in FY 1996, up 1.5 pct.

text.p: The New York City comptroller on Thursday said that in fiscal year 1996, the city spent a total of $32 billion, which amounted to 1.5 percent, or $481 million more than the previous year.

Alan Hevesi noted that city paid for most of the jump in spending as city funds, which are defined as all its revenues excluding categorical federal and state aid, rose by three percent, or $643 million.

However, the comptroller highlighted a disturbing pattern of overspending by some city agencies in the 1996 fiscal year, which ended June 30, including the Police Department, the Fire Department, and the Department of Corrections.
"There is a continuing problem of city agencies spending more than budgeted in specific units of appropriation," he said, in prepared remarks.
Hevesi explained that Mayor Rudolph Giuliani and the City Council set how much agencies can spend according to units of appropriation.
Police Department executives overspent by $582,000 for personal services, which are defined as pay and benefits.
The Fire Department's excess spending broke down into $926,000 for executive administration and $1.5 million for fire extinguishment and emergency response.
The overspending by the Department of Corrections added up to $301,000 in operations.

New York City is close to hitting its legal debt limit, which by the end of the 1997 fiscal year could prevent it from borrowing more to pay for new contracts and purchase orders for its capital program, Hevesi noted.
The city now is exploring ways of getting around the cap on debt, including setting up a new infrastructure authority.

As of September 30, 1996, New York City only had another $895 million left under the ceiling, down from $2.7 billion at the end of the 1995 fiscal year, when the debt ceiling totaled $35 billion, the comptroller said.
The debt ceiling fluctuates because it is based on the value of real estate.
The city in the 1996 fiscal year borrowed or committed to spend $29.2 billion that counted under its debt ceiling, which fell to $31.9 billion as of June 30, 1996, Hevesi said.

While real estate tax collections fell to $7.1 billion from $7.47 billion a year-ago, the deliquency rate, viewed as an important measure of fiscal health, fell to 3.8 percent in the 1996 year from the previous five percent level.

The continued improvement in the brokerage industry, a vital engine of the city's economy, helped push total tax revenues to move than $18 billion, a $428 million jump from the previous period. The largest increase was seen in income taxes, which leaped 13 percent.
And the city's five pension plans produced an overall investment return of more than 17 percent, which Hevesi said was almost double the rate assumed by actuaries.
Two negative developments included a big rise in the Water & Sewer System's allowence for uncollectible accounts and a slight drop in the surplus transferred by the Off-Track Betting Corp.

The Water & Sewer System raised the uncollectible allowance more than 100 percent to $272 million from $135 million a year-ago, while bad debt expense leaped to $317 million from $95 million. Hevesi wrote that the cost of bad debt was "the major component" in the system's operating loss, which totaled $240 million.

The Off-Track Betting Corp ended the fiscal year with a $28.6 million surplus and transferred $25.8 million of this sum to the city, slighly less than the $27.6 million the city got in the previous period.
--Joan Gralla, 212-859-1654
